title: The Egyptian Republic
subtitle: 1952–today · The Free Officers, Nasser's Arab socialism, Sadat's realignment, Mubarak's thirty years, and the 2011 revolution and the Sisi era

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The Free Officers and the republic, Nasser's Arab socialism, Sadat's realignment, Mubarak's thirty years, and the 2011 revolution, Morsi and the Sisi era

entries.label: Muhammad Naguib, figurehead president
entries.hint: The senior officer the Free Officers put in front of their coup, Naguib became the republic's first president when the monarchy was abolished in June 1953. Popular and inclined to restore parliamentary life, he lost a power struggle with Nasser over the spring of 1954 and was placed under house arrest that November, where he stayed for eighteen years. His removal settled that the revolution would be authoritarian.
entries.note: Republic proclaimed by RCC decree, 18 June 1953 (Official Gazette / al-Waqaʾiʿ al-Misriyya); Naguib, 'Kalimati lil-Tarikh' (memoir, 1975).

entries.label: Gamal Abdel Nasser and the single centre
entries.hint: Nasser won the March 1954 crisis, was confirmed president by plebiscite in 1956, and until his death in September 1970 was the unchallenged centre of the state. He nationalised the Canal, built the High Dam, led Arab nationalism, absorbed the 1967 defeat and rebuilt the army before dying of a heart attack at 52. His funeral drew perhaps five million people into Cairo's streets.
entries.note: 1956 constitution and presidential plebiscite, 23 June 1956 (Official Gazette); UAR provisional constitution 1958; R. Stephens, 'Nasser: A Political Biography' (1971).

entries.label: Anwar Sadat and the realignment
entries.hint: Sadat succeeded on Nasser's death, purged his rivals in the 1971 'Corrective Revolution', expelled the Soviet advisers in 1972, and launched the October 1973 war that let him open the economy and turn to the United States. His separate peace with Israel isolated Egypt in the Arab world; on 6 October 1981 soldiers from a jihadist cell shot him dead at the victory parade.
entries.note: Sadat, 'In Search of Identity' (1978); assassination reported to the People's Assembly, October 1981; trial of al-Jihad, 1982 (case papers).

entries.label: Hosni Mubarak's thirty years
entries.hint: Vice-president since 1975, Mubarak took over after the assassination and governed under continuous emergency law for almost thirty years. He kept the peace with Israel and the American alliance, survived the 1990s Islamist insurgency, opened the economy in stages, and by the 2000s was grooming his son Gamal to succeed him. Eighteen days of protest forced his resignation on 11 February 2011.
entries.note: Emergency Law 162/1958 renewed by presidential decree throughout the period (Official Gazette); resignation announced by Vice-President Suleiman, 11 February 2011.

entries.label: Mohamed Morsi, the elected year
entries.hint: The Muslim Brotherhood's candidate won the first free presidential election in June 2012 with 51.7 percent. His year in office was consumed by a fight with the judiciary and the old state, a rushed Islamist-tinted constitution, and a collapsing economy. Mass protests on 30 June 2013 gave the army its opening; he was removed and detained on 3 July and died in a courtroom in 2019.
entries.note: Presidential Election Commission final result, 24 June 2012 (Official Gazette); armed-forces statement of 3 July 2013 (SCAF communiqué).

entries.label: Abdel Fattah el-Sisi and the restored officers' state
entries.hint: Defence minister under Morsi, Sisi led the July 2013 removal, oversaw the interim presidency of judge Adly Mansour, and was elected president in 2014 with 96.9 percent, re-elected in 2018 and 2023. His government has combined mega-projects, IMF austerity and currency floats with the widest political repression in the republic's history, and a 2019 amendment extended presidential terms toward 2030.
entries.note: Presidential Election Commission results 2014, 2018, 2023 (Official Gazette); 2014 constitution and 2019 amendments (Official Gazette, 8 June 2014; 25 April 2019).

entries.label: The Free Officers and the Revolutionary Command Council
entries.hint: A conspiracy of about a hundred middle-ranking officers seized power on the night of 22–23 July 1952, sent King Farouk into exile within three days, and ruled through a Revolutionary Command Council of a dozen men. It abolished parties in January 1953, the monarchy in June, and by 1954 had narrowed to Nasser's personal rule. The RCC dissolved itself when the 1956 constitution came in.
entries.note: RCC Proclamation No. 1, 23 July 1952 (broadcast text, Anwar al-Sadat reading); abdication instrument of Farouk, 26 July 1952.

entries.label: The single party: Liberation Rally to ASU
entries.hint: The regime tried three official mass organisations in succession — the Liberation Rally (1953), the National Union (1957) and the Arab Socialist Union (1962) — none of them a party that could constrain the president. The ASU had committees in every village and workplace and a vanguard cadre, but it was an instrument of mobilisation and surveillance, not of rule. Sadat broke it into three 'platforms' in 1976.
entries.note: National Charter (al-Mithaq al-Watani), May 1962; Law 40/1977 on political parties (Official Gazette).

entries.label: Sadat's Corrective Revolution
entries.hint: In May 1971 Sadat arrested Ali Sabri and the Nasserist power-centre — the men who controlled the ASU, the intelligence services and the ministry of the interior — in what he called the Corrective Revolution. It let him rewrite the constitution that September, ease the police state a little, release Muslim Brothers from prison to balance the left, and set his own course toward war and the West.
entries.note: Permanent Constitution of 11 September 1971 (Official Gazette); trial of the 'centres of power', 1971–72 (case papers).

entries.label: The NDP and the succession question
entries.hint: Sadat founded the National Democratic Party in 1978 as the ruling wing of the old ASU; under Mubarak it held four-fifths of every assembly through rigged elections and patronage. In the 2000s its Policies Secretariat, run by Gamal Mubarak and a circle of businessmen, drove privatisation and looked set to inherit the presidency. Protesters burned its Nile-front headquarters on 28 January 2011.
entries.note: NDP founding declaration 1978; Supreme Administrative Court dissolution ruling, 16 April 2011 (case 22371/57).

entries.group: The Army and the Security State
entries.label: The officers' republic
entries.hint: Since 1952 the armed forces have been the state's load-bearing institution: five of the seven presidents have been officers, the defence budget and the military's own economic empire sit outside civilian audit, and the constitution reserves the defence ministry to a serving general. The army stepped aside from daily rule under Sadat and Mubarak but never from the commanding heights, and returned openly to power in 2011 and 2013.
entries.note: 2014 constitution, arts. 200–204 and 234 (Official Gazette); Y. Sayigh, 'Owners of the Republic' (Carnegie, 2019).

entries.group: The Army and the Security State
entries.label: The Mukhabarat and the Ministry of the Interior
entries.hint: The republic built a dense apparatus of control — the General Intelligence Service, the Mabahith political police, and a State Security Investigations directorate whose files covered millions. Torture in police stations, administrative detention and a parallel system of state-security courts were routine under emergency law. The burning of the SSI headquarters in March 2011 briefly exposed the archive before the service was renamed and rebuilt.
entries.note: Emergency Law 162/1958; Human Rights Watch, 'Work on Him Until He Confesses' (2011); protocols of the State Security Prosecution.

entries.group: The Army and the Security State
entries.dynasty: Supreme Council of the Armed Forces
entries.label: SCAF governs the transition
entries.hint: When Mubarak fell, a Supreme Council of the Armed Forces of about twenty senior officers, chaired by Field Marshal Tantawi, took full authority for seventeen months. It suspended the constitution, ran referendums and staggered elections, tried thousands of civilians before military courts, and issued a constitutional declaration reserving its own powers before handing the presidency to Morsi in June 2012.
entries.note: Constitutional Declaration of 13 February 2011 and Supplementary Declaration of 17 June 2012 (Official Gazette); SCAF communiqués 1–90.

entries.label: The Brotherhood as perennial opposition
entries.hint: Banned and its members jailed and hanged after 1954, tolerated as a social movement from the 1970s, the Muslim Brotherhood ran candidates as independents and by 2005 held a fifth of parliament. It was the country's only mass organisation outside the state when Mubarak fell, won the 2011–12 elections, took the presidency, lost it in 2013, and was designated a terrorist group with tens of thousands imprisoned or exiled.
entries.note: Dissolution order 1954; Cabinet decision designating the group a terrorist organisation, 25 December 2013 (Official Gazette).

entries.label: Kefaya, 6 April and the protest generation
entries.hint: From 2004 a secular protest current took shape — the Kefaya ('Enough') movement against a fifth Mubarak term and a hereditary succession, the 6 April Youth founded around the 2008 Mahalla textile strike, and campaigns like 'We are all Khaled Said' after a young man was beaten to death by police in 2010. These networks called the 25 January 2011 protest that became the revolution.
entries.note: Kefaya founding statement, 2004; '6 April' Facebook mobilisation, 2008; Khaled Said autopsy dispute, June 2010 (prosecution file).

entries.label: The licensed opposition parties
entries.hint: The 1976 opening allowed a tame multiparty life: the New Wafd revived in 1978, the leftist Tagammuʿ and the Nasserists were tolerated, and a Political Parties Committee run by the ruling party licensed or blocked the rest. Real opposition — the Brotherhood, and after 2011 parties like the Social Democrats and the Strong Egypt Party — was either banned or squeezed out, and by the 2020s parliament held almost no independent voice.
entries.note: Law 40/1977 and the Political Parties Committee; People's Assembly and House of Representatives election results, 1976–2020 (Official Gazette).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The 1956 Suez war, the 1967 defeat and the War of Attrition, the 1973 October War, the Islamist insurgency of the 1990s, and the crackdowns after 2013

entries.label: The Suez Crisis and the Tripartite Aggression
entries.loc: Port Said and the Canal Zone
entries.hint: After Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal Company in July 1956, Britain, France and Israel attacked in collusion at the end of October — Israel across Sinai, the European powers landing at Port Said on the pretext of separating the sides. American and Soviet pressure forced a humiliating Anglo-French withdrawal within weeks. Egypt lost militarily but Nasser emerged the victor of Arab nationalism.
entries.note: UN General Assembly Resolution 997 (ES-I), 2 November 1956; the Protocol of Sèvres, 24 October 1956 (released texts).

entries.label: The Yemen intervention
entries.hint: When officers overthrew Yemen's imam in 1962, Nasser sent an expeditionary force that grew to 70,000 men to defend the republicans against Saudi-backed royalists. Five years of inconclusive mountain war — later called 'Egypt's Vietnam' — drained the treasury, tied down the best units, and left the army overextended and complacent on the eve of June 1967.
entries.note: Ahram and Ministry of War communiqués 1962–67; Jesse Ferris, 'Nasser's Gamble' (2012), from Egyptian and Soviet archives.

entries.label: The Six-Day War and the loss of Sinai
entries.hint: Israel destroyed the Egyptian air force on the ground in the first hours of 5 June and overran all of Sinai to the Canal within four days. Ten to fifteen thousand Egyptian soldiers died, mostly in the retreat; the Canal closed for eight years. The defeat — al-Naksa, 'the setback' — shattered the Nasserist promise and forced the regime to rebuild around the single goal of recovering the lost land.
entries.note: UN Security Council Resolution 242, 22 November 1967; the Egyptian official inquiry into the June defeat, 1967–68.

entries.label: The War of Attrition
entries.hint: From 1968 Nasser fought a static artillery and commando war across the Canal to deny Israel a comfortable occupation, and Israel replied with deep air raids that Soviet crews and missiles were brought in to stop. The fighting killed thousands and displaced the Canal cities' population before an American-brokered ceasefire in August 1970, weeks before Nasser's death.
entries.note: Rogers Plan and ceasefire of 7 August 1970 (US State Department); Egyptian Armed Forces war communiqués.

entries.label: The October War
entries.hint: On 6 October, Yom Kippur and the tenth of Ramadan, Egyptian forces stormed across the Canal, broke the Bar-Lev Line and held a strip of Sinai against counter-attack for two weeks before an Israeli crossing encircled the Third Army. Militarily a draw, politically it restored Egyptian and Arab confidence, triggered the oil embargo, and opened the road to disengagement and negotiation.
entries.note: UN Security Council Resolution 338, 22 October 1973; Sinai I disengagement agreement, 18 January 1974.

entries.label: The Bread Intifada
entries.loc: Cairo, Alexandria and the industrial towns
entries.hint: When the government, under IMF pressure, cut subsidies on bread, flour and cooking oil, hundreds of thousands poured into the streets of every major city for two days, attacking symbols of privilege and chanting against Sadat. The army restored order after perhaps 80 deaths, the price rises were withdrawn, and the regime learned that the subsidy on bread was politically untouchable.
entries.note: Ministry of Interior casualty figures, January 1977; People's Assembly debate and the withdrawal of Decree 66/1977.

entries.label: The Islamist insurgency of the 1990s
entries.hint: The Gamaʿa al-Islamiyya and Islamic Jihad waged an armed campaign against the state, Coptic Christians, secular writers and tourists, concentrated in the poor towns of Asyut and Minya. The state answered with mass arrests, military courts, executions and collective punishment of villages. The 1997 massacre of 58 tourists at Luxor broke public sympathy; a jailed leadership declared a ceasefire in 1999.
entries.note: State Information Service security bulletins; the Gamaʿa's 1999 'Initiative to Halt Violence'; Human Rights Watch reporting 1993–99.

entries.label: The 25 January Revolution
entries.hint: A protest called for Police Day grew within days into a nationwide occupation of the streets; the 'Friday of Rage' on 28 January burned police stations and the ruling-party headquarters and drove the police from the cities. Eighteen days of protest, some 850 dead, a failed regime counter-attack by hired men on camels and horses, and the army's refusal to fire ended in Mubarak's resignation.
entries.note: National Council for Human Rights fact-finding report, 2011; Fact-Finding Commission on the events, decree 294/2011.

entries.label: The 2013 removal and the Rabaa dispersal
entries.hint: After the army removed President Morsi on 3 July 2013, his supporters occupied two Cairo squares for six weeks. On 14 August security forces cleared the Rabaa al-Adawiya sit-in by force, killing at least 800 people in a single day — one of the largest killings of demonstrators in modern history. A wave of church burnings, mass death sentences and a designation of the Brotherhood as terrorist followed.
entries.note: Human Rights Watch, 'All According to Plan: The Rabaa Massacre' (2014); official Fact-Finding Committee report, 2014.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The 1953 republic and its successive constitutions, the single-party state and its managed opening, emergency law, the public sector, and the security state

entries.label: The republic and its many constitutions
entries.hint: The republic has lived under nine constitutional texts — the 1953 declaration, the 1956, 1958 (UAR) and 1964 charters, Sadat's 'permanent' constitution of 1971, the SCAF declarations of 2011, and the constitutions of 2012, 2014 and its 2019 amendments. Each concentrated power in the presidency; each was ratified by lopsided referendum; and the 2019 amendments extended Sisi's eligibility toward 2030 and wrote in a military guardianship role.
entries.note: Constitutional texts in al-Jarida al-Rasmiyya (1956, 1971, 2012, 2014, 2019); referendum results, State Information Service.

entries.label: Emergency law as the normal condition
entries.hint: Law 162 of 1958 lets the president rule by decree, detain without charge, and refer civilians to exceptional courts. It was in force almost continuously from 1967, and without interruption from Sadat's assassination in 1981 until 2012. Formally lifted after the revolution, its powers were rebuilt through the 2013 protest law, terrorism legislation and a 2017 re-declaration renewed every three months for years.
entries.note: Emergency Law 162/1958 and Law 12/2017 amendments (Official Gazette); presidential renewal decrees 2017–2021.

entries.label: The July Decrees and sequestration
entries.hint: In July 1961 a burst of decree-laws nationalised the banks, insurance companies, and most large industry and commerce, capped landholding again, and imposed a steep progressive tax. A wave of sequestration seized the property of hundreds of families deemed enemies of the revolution. Within a year the state owned the commanding heights, and a managerial class dependent on the regime had replaced the old propertied elite.
entries.note: Laws 117–119 of 1961 and the sequestration decrees (Official Gazette, July 1961); Charter of National Action, 1962.

entries.label: The public sector and the graduate guarantee
entries.hint: From 1961 the state guaranteed a government job to every university and higher-institute graduate, and later to technical-school leavers. The bureaucracy swelled past three million, the public-sector companies overstaffed to absorb the rest, and a lifetime of low pay, security and side income became the middle-class norm. Hiring was frozen in the 1980s but the expectation, and the overstaffed ministries, remained.
entries.note: Law 14/1964 on graduate appointment; CAPMAS public-employment series; J. Waterbury, 'The Egypt of Nasser and Sadat' (1983).

entries.label: The judiciary between independence and the executive
entries.hint: Nasser purged some 200 judges in the 1969 'massacre of the judiciary' for resisting single-party control. Sadat created a Supreme Constitutional Court that in the 1980s and 1990s struck down election laws and defended property rights. Judges' associations pressed for full independence in 2005–06; after 2013 the executive gained powers to pick court heads, and terrorism-circuit courts issued mass death sentences.
entries.note: Presidential decrees of August 1969; Law 48/1979 on the Supreme Constitutional Court; Law 13/2017 on judicial appointments.

entries.label: The 'state of institutions' and the managed opening
entries.hint: Sadat promised a 'state of institutions and law' after 1971 — a real constitution, an end to sequestration, the return of the courts. He split the Arab Socialist Union into three 'platforms' in 1976 and licensed them as parties in 1977, reviving a limited pluralism. But a 1978 'Law of Shame', press controls and the mass arrests of September 1981 showed the opening's limits.
entries.note: Law 40/1977 on political parties; Law 95/1980 ('Law of Shame'); the September 1981 arrest decrees (Official Gazette).

entries.label: The legal architecture of repression after 2013
entries.hint: A protest law in November 2013 made unauthorised gatherings punishable by prison; a 2015 counter-terrorism law defined terrorism broadly and shielded soldiers from prosecution; a 2017 NGO law, replaced in 2019, put civil society under security-service licensing; and pre-trial detention was stretched for years by 'recycling' defendants into new cases. Tens of thousands were held as political prisoners.
entries.note: Law 107/2013 (protest); Law 94/2015 (counter-terrorism); Laws 70/2017 and 149/2019 (associations); Egyptian Front for Human Rights case tracking.

entries.label: The informal order of the neighbourhood
entries.hint: Where the state's reach thinned — the unplanned quarters that house most Cairenes, the villages, the markets — order ran on other channels: the wasta (connection) that got a permit or a job, the local strongman and his baltagiyya (toughs) hired by candidates at election time, the mosque and the family. The 2011 security collapse showed how much daily governance had always been informal.
entries.note: D. Singerman, 'Avenues of Participation' (1995); Sims, 'Understanding Cairo' (2010); ISS and TIMEP reporting on baltagiyya, 2011–13.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Al-Azhar and the state, the Muslim Brotherhood between repression and toleration, the Coptic Church under Shenouda and Tawadros, and the Islamic revival and the Salafi current

entries.label: Al-Azhar nationalised
entries.hint: Law 103 of 1961 turned the thousand-year-old mosque-university into a state body: the president appoints the Shaykh al-Azhar, the government funds it, and it gained modern faculties of medicine and engineering alongside the religious sciences. It became the regime's instrument for a moderate official Islam — endorsing peace with Israel, family planning and, after 2013, the removal of Morsi — while guarding its own doctrinal autonomy.
entries.note: Law 103/1961 reorganising al-Azhar (Official Gazette); M. Zeghal, 'Gardiens de l'Islam' (1996).

entries.label: The Brotherhood: from the gallows to the daʿwa
entries.hint: After a 1954 assassination attempt on Nasser, the Brotherhood was crushed — thousands jailed, six leaders hanged, and in 1966 the writer Sayyid Qutb executed. Released under Sadat, it renounced violence and rebuilt as a social movement running clinics, syndicates and charities, and by the 2000s was the strongest force in civil society. Its brief hold on power in 2012–13 ended in the deadliest repression of its history.
entries.note: Trial of the Muslim Brotherhood, 1954 (case papers); R. Mitchell, 'The Society of the Muslim Brothers' (1969); C. Wickham, 'The Muslim Brotherhood' (2013).

entries.label: The Coptic Church as a communal state
entries.hint: Pope Shenouda III (1971–2012) rebuilt the Coptic Orthodox Church into the effective political and social representative of Egypt's Christians — running courts of personal status, negotiating directly with the president, and mobilising the vote. His clash with Sadat led to internal exile in 1981–85. His successor Tawadros II backed the 2013 change of power, binding the Church still more tightly to the state.
entries.note: Presidential Decree 5/1981 (Shenouda's confinement); S. Ibrahim et al., 'The Copts of Egypt' (1996); church statements of July 2013.

entries.label: The Islamic revival
entries.hint: From the 1970s a broad re-Islamisation reshaped daily life: the hijab returned first among students and spread across classes, thousands of private 'popular' mosques opened outside state control, Islamic banking and welfare associations grew, and cassette-sermon preachers and later satellite televangelists reached mass audiences. It was cultural before it was political, and it cut across the Brotherhood and the state alike.
entries.note: S. Mahmood, 'Politics of Piety' (2005); G. Starrett, 'Putting Islam to Work' (1998); CAPMAS mosque registration data.

entries.label: Sufism and the moulids under the republic
entries.hint: For millions, faith still centred on the Sufi order and the saint's festival: the moulid of Sayyid al-Badawi at Tanta drew crowds in the millions, and the state's Supreme Council of Sufi Orders licensed some seventy-odd tariqas. Salafi and modernist pressure branded the shrine visits and the moulid superstition, and from the 2000s the state restricted the festivals on security and, later, public-health grounds.
entries.note: Law 118/1976 on Sufi orders; S. Mayeur-Jaouen, 'Histoire d'un pèlerinage légendaire en islam' (2004); Ministry of Awqaf moulid circulars.

entries.label: The Salafi current and the Nour Party
entries.hint: A Saudi-influenced Salafi movement grew from the 1980s around the Alexandria-based 'Salafi Call', preaching scriptural literalism and, until 2011, staying out of politics. After the revolution it founded the Nour Party, which stunned observers by taking a quarter of the 2011–12 parliamentary vote. Nour then backed the 2013 removal of Morsi, and has survived as the regime's tolerated Islamist face.
entries.note: al-Daʿwa al-Salafiyya publications; High Elections Commission results, January 2012 (Official Gazette); S. Lacroix, 'Sheikhs and Politicians' (2012).

entries.label: Sectarian violence and the 'national unity' formula
entries.hint: Communal violence recurred — a burned church at al-Khanka in 1972, the Zawiya al-Hamra killings of 1981, repeated attacks in Upper Egypt, the 2011 New Year bombing of the Two Saints Church in Alexandria that killed 23, and church bombings by Islamic State cells after 2016. The state answered with a rhetoric of 'national unity', informal 'reconciliation sessions' that denied justice, and slow church-building permits eased only by a 2016 law.
entries.note: Report of the committee on the al-Khanka events, 1972; Law 80/2016 on church construction; EIPR sectarian-incident database.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Naguib Mahfouz and the Nobel, the golden age of cinema and song, state and satellite television, and the culture of the 2011 generation

entries.label: Naguib Mahfouz and the Nobel Prize
entries.hint: Mahfouz published the 'Cairo Trilogy' in 1956–57, a realist chronicle of a Gamaliya family across the national movement, and became the anchor of the modern Arabic novel. His 1959 allegory 'Children of Gebelawi' was banned by al-Azhar and never sold openly in Egypt. He won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1988 — the first Arabic-language laureate — and in 1994 survived a stabbing by an Islamist who had judged the old novel blasphemous.
entries.note: Swedish Academy Nobel citation, 1988; al-Azhar Islamic Research Academy ruling on 'Awlad Haratina', 1959; police report on the 1994 attack.

entries.label: The studio, the golden age, and the private revival
entries.hint: Egyptian cinema, already the Arab world's Hollywood, was nationalised in 1963 and produced a socially serious 'golden age' under directors like Youssef Chahine and Salah Abu Seif. The public sector's decline, video and a Gulf-funded taste for 'clean' comedy shrank it in the 1980s–90s before a private commercial revival. Cairo's films and stars still set the register of spoken Arabic across the region.
entries.note: Law establishing the General Egyptian Cinema Organisation, 1963; V. Shafik, 'Arab Cinema' (1998); annual production figures, National Film Centre.

entries.label: Umm Kulthum and the era of the long song
entries.hint: On the first Thursday of every month Umm Kulthum's live radio concert stopped the Arab world; her hour-long songs, and Abdel Halim Hafez's nationalist anthems, made the state broadcaster the voice of the nation. Her 1967–73 fundraising tours after the defeat raised money and morale. Her funeral in 1975 drew crowds rivalling Nasser's, and marked the end of the classical Egyptian song's dominance.
entries.note: Egyptian Radio recordings and concert logs, 1952–73; V. Danielson, 'The Voice of Egypt' (1997).

entries.label: Television drama and the vernacular stage
entries.hint: Television arrived in 1960 and the musalsal — the Ramadan serial — became the country's central shared narrative, its historical epics and social dramas watched from Morocco to Iraq. The 1960s also produced a sharp colloquial theatre and the poets Salah Jahin and Fuʾad Haddad, who wrote a national sensibility in Egyptian Arabic. State production later gave way to Gulf-financed private networks.
entries.note: Egyptian Television founding, 21 July 1960; Jahin, 'al-Rubaʿiyyat' (1963); Arab Radio and Television Union viewership surveys.

entries.label: The press: from al-Ahram to media consolidation
entries.hint: Nasser nationalised the press in 1960; Mohamed Hassanein Heikal's al-Ahram became a quasi-official record and a research powerhouse. Party and then independent papers — al-Wafd, al-Dustour, al-Masry al-Youm — reopened space from the 1980s, and satellite channels and blogs widened it in the 2000s. After 2013 security-linked companies bought up the major private outlets and the space closed again.
entries.note: Press nationalisation decree, May 1960; Reporters Without Borders and CPJ Egypt files; Mada Masr reporting on media ownership, 2017–19.

entries.label: The 2011 generation: graffiti, mahraganat and satire
entries.hint: The years around the revolution produced a distinct urban culture: the Mohamed Mahmoud Street murals of the martyrs, the electro-shaʿbi 'mahraganat' music born in the working-class quarters, and Bassem Youssef's satirical show that drew tens of millions before it was pulled in 2014. Much of it moved online and much was later suppressed, but mahraganat became the country's dominant popular sound.
entries.note: Documentation of the Mohamed Mahmoud murals (AUC archive); Musicians' Syndicate ban on mahraganat performers, 2020; broadcast records of 'al-Bernameg', 2011–14.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Arab nationalism and its disillusion, the Islamist intellectual turn, the leftist and liberal currents, feminism, and the economists' critique of the state

entries.label: Arab nationalism and the disillusion of 1967
entries.hint: Nasser's short 'Philosophy of the Revolution' (1954) placed Egypt at the centre of Arab, African and Islamic 'circles', and the 1962 National Charter set out an Arab socialism of the non-Western path. The June 1967 defeat broke the spell: a literature of self-criticism — Sadiq al-ʿAzm, Tawfiq al-Hakim's 'Return of Consciousness' — asked how the rhetoric had hidden the rot, and opened the door to both the Islamist and liberal reactions.
entries.note: G. A. Nasser, 'Falsafat al-Thawra' (1954); al-Hakim, 'ʿAwdat al-Waʿi' (1974); S. J. al-ʿAzm, 'al-Naqd al-Dhati baʿd al-Hazima' (1968).

entries.label: The Marxist current and the student left
entries.hint: Egypt's communists dissolved their own party in 1965 to join the Arab Socialist Union, a decision long debated as surrender. A new student left drove the protests of 1968 and 1972–73 that pushed Sadat toward war, and produced intellectuals and the journal group around 'al-Taliʿa'. Repression, the rise of the Islamist campus and the collapse of the model abroad had marginalised it by the 1980s.
entries.note: 'Hall al-ahzab al-shuyuʿiyya', 1965; A. Abdalla, 'The Student Movement and National Politics in Egypt' (1985).

entries.label: Sayyid Qutb's Milestones and its afterlife
entries.hint: Written in prison and published in 1964, Qutb's 'Milestones' argued that Muslim societies had reverted to pagan ignorance (jahiliyya) and that a vanguard must wage struggle to restore God's sovereignty. He was hanged in 1966. The book became the founding text of the militant current — al-Jihad, the Gamaʿa, and later al-Qaʿida drew on it — while the Brotherhood's mainstream spent decades arguing its way out of his conclusions.
entries.note: S. Qutb, 'Maʿalim fi al-Tariq' (1964); verdict of the State Security Court, August 1966; G. Kepel, 'Le Prophète et Pharaon' (1984).

entries.label: Feminism and the rights movement
entries.hint: Doria Shafik's 'Bint al-Nil' won women the vote in 1956 before Nasser jailed the independent women's groups. State feminism gave women education, work and, in 1979 and 2000, personal-status reform, while independent voices — Nawal El Saadawi's writing on the body and patriarchy, banned and prosecuted — pushed further. From the 1990s a set of rights organisations carried the argument until the post-2013 closure of civil society.
entries.note: 1956 constitution, art. 31 (women's suffrage); N. El Saadawi, 'al-Wajh al-ʿAri lil-Marʾa al-ʿArabiyya' (1977); decree-law 44/1979 on personal status.

entries.label: The critique of the state economy
entries.hint: As the Nasserist model frayed, economists mapped what replaced it: the parasitic 'open-door' bourgeoisie (ʿAdil Husayn, Galal Amin), the vast informal economy that employed most new workers, and the social costs of structural adjustment. Galal Amin's popular 'Whatever Happened to the Egyptians?' (1998) read the whole transformation through consumption, migration and class anxiety, and sold for decades.
entries.note: G. Amin, 'Madha Hadatha lil-Misriyyin?' (1998); ILO informal-sector studies from the 1990s; ʿA. Husayn, 'al-Iqtisad al-Misri' (1982).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Land reform and nationalisation, the High Dam economy, Sadat's infitah, structural adjustment and privatisation, Gulf remittances, and the IMF era

categories.label: Technology
